title: Adaptive output slicing and client ergonomics — PRD (WIP)
body:
Status: WIP — brainstorming + first-pass API sketches.

Quick summary
- Problem: hosted streaming responses today are either full-fidelity (higher latency/cost) or cheap partials. We need a predictable developer model for progressive fidelity + tool-calls.
- Proposal: introduce an adaptive output slicing protocol + SDK ergonomics guidelines so clients can consume progressive chunks that vary by fidelity (summary -> details -> tool-annotated payloads) and gracefully handle tool-calls and structured outputs.

Goals
- Make progressive/partial responses safe and predictable for app developers (avoid flicker, duplicates, missing fields).
- Improve tail-latency and perceived responsiveness for interactive flows by surfacing lower-fidelity slices early.
- Preserve correctness for tool-calls: the SDK should provide clear semantics for when tool calls occur in-flight, how to pause/resume, and how to reconcile structured outputs.
- Limit server-side complexity: runtime should leverage existing streaming hooks and add a lightweight framing layer.

Non-goals
- Full design for multi-model composition (out of scope for this doc).
- Replacing existing typed-output APIs in one big migration — aim for opt-in flags and backward compat.

Background / motivation (notes from user interviews)
- Product teams want UX where first token appears in <200ms and a structured action appears soon after.
- Many apps show a brief summary while waiting for a long-form result; developers currently implement brittle heuristics on the client.
- Tool-call races: clients struggle when the model starts a tool-call mid-stream; sometimes the client already displayed user-facing content based on incomplete context.

High-level design
1) Output slices: a response is composed of 1..N slices. Each slice has: slice_type (summary | content | annotation | action), fidelity_hint (low|medium|high), stable_id (client-visible id to dedup), and optional schema_hint (json-schema id or type tag). Slices stream as discrete frames.
2) Framing: extend existing incremental output frames with a small header that includes slice_type and stable_id. Body remains text or encoded structured payload. Keep frame sizes small and allow partial text continuation frames.
3) Tool-calls: a special slice_type=action indicates a tool invocation is being initiated. The action-slice can include: tool_name (recommended), input_snippet, and expected_result_schema_hint. When a tool-slice is emitted, the SDK should: a) pause delivery of subsequent content slices meant for user-facing UI until tool completes OR b) mark those slices as tentative with explicit flag so client can choose to hide.
4) Structured output: schema_hint allows server to annotate slices with a lightweight schema pointer (string). Clients can request strict-mode where the server enforces that final high-fidelity slices validate against the schema before marking response complete.

API sketch (hosted REST/websocket + SDK ergonomics)
- Query parameters (opt-in): output_slicing=adaptive|disabled|summary_first, slice_timeout_ms=200 (how long to wait before emitting a lower-fidelity slice), client_mode=graceful|strict.
- Response frames (example JSON-ish frame header; payload may be plain text or base64 JSON):
  {
    "frame_type": "slice",
    "slice_id": "s-5a3f",
    "slice_type": "summary",
    "fidelity_hint": "low",
    "schema_hint": "urn:jobs.v1.summary?ver=1"
  }
  <payload bytes>
- SDK should provide a SliceReader abstraction: on_slice(fn(slice_meta, payload, commit_callback)). commit_callback lets the app confirm display of a tentative slice or instruct SDK to suppress if later invalidated by a high-fidelity replacement.

Client ergonomics rules (developer patterns)
- Default: very small summary slice emitted quickly (<200ms), followed by progressively richer slices. Clients show summary in a collapsed UI and expand when higher-fidelity arrives.
- Tentative content: any slice emitted while a tool action is pending must be marked tentative. SDK exposes "tentative" boolean. Apps should not create irreversible side-effects based on tentative slices (e.g., not persist to DB).
- Dedup: stable_id used to dedupe repeated slices across reconnections or multi-path routing. If a higher-fidelity slice with same stable_id arrives, it replaces the previous content in-place.
- Partial schema binding: if schema_hint present, SDK offers a convenience method parse_schema(schema_hint, payload) -> either typed object or error. For strict-mode, SDK refuses to surface final completion until parse succeeds.

Tool-calling behavioral contract
- Signals: tool-action-slice emitted when model intends to call a tool. Two-step flow: ACTION_INIT -> ACTION_RESULT. ACTION_INIT contains tool_name, input_snippet, expected_result_schema. ACTION_RESULT contains the tool output as a slice (slice_type=annotation or action-result).
- Backpressure: when ACTION_INIT emitted, server can optionally pause further model tokens until tool result available (configurable per-request). Developer can choose: immediate-summaries-only (client_mode=graceful) vs block-until-tool (client_mode=strict).
- Idempotency: tool invocations must include invocation_id. SDK surfaces this so the client can track in-flight tool calls and avoid duplicate side effects.

Structured output and reconciliation
- Progressive validation: simple syntactic validation on earlier slices, full semantic validation on final slice. Provide explicit transition slice (slice_type=commit) when server believes output stable.
- Merge strategy: when a high-fidelity slice arrives and conflicts with prior tentative content, SDK exposes a merge hook that offers (replace|patch|annotate) options. Default: replace in-place to keep UI simple.

Telemetry & observability
- Emit per-slice telemetry: slice_type, fidelity_hint, latency_ms (time from request to slice emission), tool_call_flag, invocation_id, schema_hint, validation_status.
- Console: per-route charts for slice-rate, average time-to-summary, tool-wait-time, percent of responses with tentative slices.

Edge cases and failure modes
- Tool fails or times out: emit action-result slice with error payload; also emit a follow-up content slice marked tentative-fallback. Client should show a graceful fallback and surface retry options.
- Partial connectivity: if socket disconnects, stable_id + slice index allow client to resume and dedupe. We should define a resume-window and retention TTL for slices (e.g., 5 minutes).
- Schema drift: model thinks it will return schema X but final output violates it. In strict-mode, mark response failed and provide diagnostics. In graceful-mode, surface best-effort with warning.

Runtime considerations (notes for serving-runtime team)
- Minimal framing layer (lightweight header per slice) to avoid adding heavy parsing work in runtime. Should be implementable as a filter in the HTTP streaming path or as a socket frame on websocket.
- Batching: prefer to keep slice emission orthogonal to token batching; slices are meta-level grouping, underlying token stream remains optimizable.
- KV cache: slice boundaries may align with cached prefixes; useful to reuse summary slices for common prompts.

Migration path / backward compat
- Default is disabled. Opt-in via request param or SDK flag. Old clients continue to get legacy streaming chunks.
- Provide SDK vN compatibility layer that translates legacy streaming chunks into a single content slice with fidelity_hint=high so older clients still readable.

Open questions / TODOs
- What default slice_timeout_ms should be? Quick experiment: 150-250ms. Need A/B test.
- resume-window retention TTL tradeoffs vs memory for runtime. Start with 5 minutes, measure.
- Exact wire encoding: simple JSON header + raw payload vs compact binary header. We need perf numbers.
- SDK ergonomics: should we auto-merge by default or require explicit commit? UX research needed.
- Interaction with rate-limiting and quotas: how to bill for tentative slices? Per emitted token seems simplest but might surprise customers.

Rollout plan (rough)
- Phase 0 (1 sprint): prototype framing on websocket and HTTP streaming in staging; basic SDK SliceReader in JS.
- Phase 1 (2-3 sprints): opt-in flag in hosted API, telemetry, basic console charts. Invite 3 internal customers.
- Phase 2 (2 sprints): SDK ergonomics polish, adds resume semantics, support for strict-mode, docs + migration guide.
- Phase 3: public beta then GA after telemetry confirms improved perceived latency without spike in support tickets.

Notes / quick sketches (brain dump)
- UX pattern: show skeleton + summary, spinner replaced by content patches. Avoid shifting layout: reveal updated text in-place.
- For tool-calls: consider a "tool block" UI component — visually shows tool name and progress; final result inlined when received.
- Danger: clients doing real side-effects (create ticket, send email) on tentative slices. Need stronger guidance and SDK safeguards. Maybe require opt-in to allow side-effect auto-commit.

Next steps (short)
- Run perf test: JSON header vs binary header throughput. @infra please allocate a small job. (Liam + Jose)
- Write SDK SliceReader prototype (JS) and a minimal React demo to test UI patterns. (Priya)
- Draft docs + migration guidance for partners. (Maya)

References / related tickets
- RED-6743 (design spike: progressive-summary-first)
- GitHub: /console PR 412 (streaming socket improvements)
- Linear: AI-321 experimental notes

End notes
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: prefer small opt-in surface + clear client semantics over a large monolithic redesign.
- Feedback welcome — add inline comments or ping me on #product-hosted-api.
